result.topic_en: The page examines when the integral formula $\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{xX}{x-a}d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{xA}{x-a}d\theta$ holds, distinguishing the cases where the modulus of a is greater than, equal to, or less than the modulus of x, and concludes that $A=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{x}{x-a}X\,d\theta$.

Value of the integral when $|x|>|a|$ (an instance of the Cauchy integral formula)
